title: Essentials of Networking
subtitle: 20 questions across VLANs, subnetting and IPv6, firewalls and ACLs, VPNs, and troubleshooting

gradeLabels.f: F-RANK -- Back to the Patch Panel

questions.q: An 802.1Q trunk port adds a 4-byte tag to Ethernet frames. Which field inside that tag identifies the VLAN?
questions.note: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag containing a 12-bit VLAN ID (VID) that can represent VLANs 1-4094.

explain.correct: The VLAN Identifier (VID) is the 12-bit field within the 802.1Q tag that specifies which VLAN the frame belongs to, supporting up to 4094 VLANs.
wrong: DSCP is a Layer 3 QoS marking in the IP header, not part of the 802.1Q VLAN tag.
EtherType 0x8100 is the 2-byte value that signals the frame carries an 802.1Q tag, but it is not the field that identifies the VLAN number.
The 3-bit Class of Service (CoS) bits are also in the 802.1Q tag and carry QoS priority, not the VLAN ID.

questions.q: A switch port configured as an access port is assigned to VLAN 20. What happens to frames leaving that port toward the end device?
options: Frames carry an 802.1Q tag for VLAN 20
Frames are dropped unless the device requests a tag
questions.note: Access ports strip the VLAN tag before sending; the connected device sees a normal untagged Ethernet frame.

explain.correct: An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN and always sends frames untagged so that ordinary end devices (which do not understand 802.1Q) receive standard Ethernet frames.
wrong: Tagged frames are sent only on trunk ports, not access ports.
Access ports do not require the end device to request anything; they simply forward untagged frames.
Double-tagging (QinQ, 802.1ad) is used for carrier Ethernet services, not standard switch access ports.

questions.q: Port security is configured on a switch port with violation mode restrict. What happens when an unauthorized MAC address is detected?
options: The frame is silently dropped with no notification
The frame is dropped and a log/SNMP trap is generated
The port is placed into err-disable state
The port flushes its MAC table and allows the new address
questions.note: Restrict drops the violating frame AND increments the violation counter, logs the event, and sends an SNMP trap -- but leaves the port up.

explain.correct: In restrict mode the switch drops frames from unauthorized MAC addresses and generates a syslog message and SNMP trap, but the port remains operationally up.
wrong: Silent drop with no notification describes protect mode, not restrict mode.
Placing the port into err-disable state describes shutdown mode, which is the most severe violation action.
Flushing the MAC table and allowing the new address is not a valid port security violation mode; it would defeat the security purpose entirely.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses are available in the subnet 192.168.10.64/26?
questions.note: A /26 gives 2^6 = 64 addresses; subtract network and broadcast = 62 usable hosts.

explain.correct: A /26 prefix leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 total addresses. Subtracting the network address (.64) and broadcast address (.127) gives 62 usable host addresses.
wrong: 30 usable hosts corresponds to a /27 prefix (2^5 - 2 = 30), not a /26.
64 is the total number of addresses in the block, not the usable host count; the network and broadcast addresses are not assignable.
126 usable hosts corresponds to a /25 prefix (2^7 - 2 = 126), not a /26.

questions.q: Which RFC 1918 private address range uses a /12 default prefix, covering 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255?
questions.note: RFC 1918 defines three private ranges: 10/8, 172.16/12, and 192.168/16. The /12 block is 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255.

explain.correct: RFC 1918 reserves 172.16.0.0/12 as private address space, which spans from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 -- a range of 1,048,576 addresses.
wrong: 10.0.0.0/8 is also an RFC 1918 private range but uses an /8 prefix covering 16.7 million addresses, not the /12 range.
192.168.0.0/16 is the third RFC 1918 private range, offering 65,536 addresses with a /16 prefix.
169.254.0.0/16 is the APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) range defined in RFC 3927, not an RFC 1918 private range.

questions.q: An IPv6 address begins with fe80::1. Which address type is this, and what is its routing behavior?
options: Global Unicast Address (GUA) -- routable on the internet
Unique Local Address -- routable within an organization
Multicast address -- sent to a group of nodes
Link-Local Address (LLA) -- not routable beyond the local link
questions.note: fe80::/10 defines the Link-Local Address range; these addresses are auto-configured and never forwarded by routers.

explain.correct: Link-Local Addresses in the fe80::/10 range are automatically assigned to every IPv6-enabled interface. Routers do not forward them beyond the local link segment.
wrong: Global Unicast Addresses use the 2000::/3 prefix range and are globally routable on the internet; fe80:: does not fall in that range.
Unique Local Addresses use the fc00::/7 prefix (fc00:: or fd00::) and are analogous to RFC 1918 private addresses, not link-local.
Multicast addresses use the ff00::/8 prefix; fe80:: is not a multicast range.

questions.q: In IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), what is the purpose of Duplicate Address Detection (DAD)?
options: To request an IPv6 address from a DHCPv6 server
To advertise the default gateway prefix to all hosts
To verify that the self-generated address is not already in use on the link
To translate IPv6 addresses to IPv4 for internet access
questions.note: Before using a SLAAC-generated address, the host sends a Neighbor Solicitation to check for duplicates -- this is DAD.

explain.correct: After generating a tentative address from the router-advertised prefix, the host performs DAD by sending a Neighbor Solicitation message. If no reply is received, the address is considered unique and activated.
wrong: Requesting an address from a DHCPv6 server describes stateful DHCPv6, not SLAAC with DAD.
Advertising the default gateway prefix is the role of the router sending a Router Advertisement (RA), not DAD.
Translating IPv6 to IPv4 describes NAT64, which is a separate mechanism unrelated to DAD.

questions.q: A standard IPv4 ACL (numbered 1-99) filters traffic based only on source IP address. Where should a standard ACL be applied to avoid blocking legitimate traffic on transit segments?
options: As close to the destination as possible
As close to the source as possible
On every router interface in the path
questions.note: Standard ACLs lack destination awareness, so placing them near the destination limits the scope of what traffic they block.

explain.correct: Because a standard ACL can only match the source address and not the destination, applying it near the destination ensures that traffic is permitted on all legitimate intermediate paths and only filtered at the final hop.
wrong: Applying close to the source is the recommended placement for extended ACLs (100-199), which can match both source and destination and therefore safely filter early.
Applying on every interface would over-filter and could block traffic that should be permitted to other destinations.
Internet-facing placement is a general firewall practice but is not the specific rule for standard ACL placement.

questions.q: An extended ACL entry uses the wildcard mask 0.0.0.255 to match a subnet. Which subnet mask does this wildcard correspond to?
questions.note: Wildcard mask = bitwise inverse of the subnet mask. 255.255.255.0 inverted = 0.0.0.255, so this matches any host in the /24 block.

explain.correct: A wildcard mask is the bitwise inverse (complement) of the subnet mask. Inverting 255.255.255.0 gives 0.0.0.255, meaning the last octet is a wildcard (any value), which matches all 256 addresses in a /24 subnet.
wrong: /32 uses subnet mask 255.255.255.255, whose inverse is 0.0.0.0 -- a wildcard that matches exactly one host.
/8 uses subnet mask 255.0.0.0, whose inverse is 0.255.255.255 -- a far larger wildcard than 0.0.0.255.
/16 uses subnet mask 255.255.0.0, whose inverse is 0.0.255.255 -- matching any host in a /16 block.

questions.q: A firewall that tracks the state of active TCP connections and automatically permits return traffic for established sessions is called a:
questions.note: Stateful firewalls maintain a connection table so return traffic matching an existing session is allowed without explicit rules.

explain.correct: A stateful inspection firewall maintains a state table of active connections. When a host initiates a TCP session, the firewall records it and automatically permits the return packets, reducing the need for separate inbound rules.
wrong: A packet-filtering firewall evaluates each packet independently against ACL rules using only header fields (IP, port, flags) with no awareness of session state.
An NGFW is a stateful firewall with added capabilities such as deep packet inspection, application-layer filtering, and integrated IPS -- it is a superset, not the baseline definition.
A proxy firewall operates at the application layer, acting as an intermediary between clients and servers, which is a different mechanism from stateful inspection.

questions.q: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is used to host public-facing servers such as web and email servers. What is the primary security purpose of a DMZ?
options: To encrypt all traffic between the internet and internal servers
To isolate public-facing servers so that a compromise does not grant direct access to the internal network
To provide NAT translation for all outbound internet traffic
To terminate VPN tunnels from remote users
questions.note: The DMZ sits between two firewalls; public servers are reachable from the internet but separated from the trusted internal LAN.

explain.correct: A DMZ places public-facing servers in a network segment between an outer firewall (internet-facing) and an inner firewall (internal network). If a server in the DMZ is compromised, the attacker still faces the inner firewall before reaching internal resources.
wrong: Encrypting traffic is the function of VPNs or TLS, not the architectural purpose of a DMZ.
NAT translation is performed by routers or firewalls and is a separate function; a DMZ can exist independently of NAT.
VPN tunnel termination can occur at a firewall or VPN concentrator but is not what defines or motivates the creation of a DMZ.

questions.q: A remote worker needs to access company resources over the internet. The company wants all internet traffic -- including non-work browsing -- to route through the corporate network for inspection. Which VPN configuration achieves this?
questions.note: Full tunnel sends ALL client traffic through the VPN; split tunnel only routes corporate-destined traffic through the tunnel.

explain.correct: A full tunnel (also called full-split disabled) configuration routes all of the remote client's internet traffic through the VPN tunnel, allowing the corporate network to inspect and filter every packet.
wrong: Split tunnel routes only traffic destined for corporate resources through the VPN, while general internet traffic exits the client's local ISP connection directly -- the opposite of what is needed here.
A site-to-site VPN connects two fixed network locations (branch to headquarters) and is not used for individual remote worker access.
An SSL portal VPN provides browser-based access to specific web applications through a web portal and does not route all client traffic.

questions.q: In 802.1X port-based Network Access Control, which device acts as the authenticator?
options: The switch or wireless access point
questions.note: The 802.1X roles are: supplicant (client), authenticator (switch/AP), authentication server (RADIUS). The authenticator enforces access based on RADIUS decisions.

explain.correct: In 802.1X, the switch or wireless access point acts as the authenticator. It intercepts the supplicant's connection attempt, forwards EAP credentials to the RADIUS server, and enforces port access based on the server's accept or reject response.
wrong: The end-user laptop is the supplicant -- the entity requesting access whose credentials are being verified.
The RADIUS server is the authentication server -- it stores credentials and makes the accept/reject decision but does not directly control port access.
The DNS server is not part of the 802.1X authentication framework.

questions.q: WPA3-Personal uses which handshake mechanism to replace the WPA2-Personal 4-way handshake and provide resistance to offline dictionary attacks?
questions.note: WPA3-Personal replaces PSK authentication with SAE (Dragonfly), which provides forward secrecy and is resistant to offline dictionary attacks.

explain.correct: WPA3-Personal uses the Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) handshake, derived from the Dragonfly key exchange. SAE provides mutual authentication and Perfect Forward Secrecy, eliminating the vulnerability to offline dictionary attacks that affected WPA2-PSK.
wrong: TKIP was the encryption protocol introduced with WPA (the interim fix after WEP). It is deprecated and not used in WPA3.
AES-CCMP is the encryption cipher used in WPA2 (and also in WPA3), but it describes the encryption algorithm, not the authentication handshake mechanism.
PEAP (Protected EAP) is used in WPA2-Enterprise and WPA3-Enterprise for 802.1X authentication, not in the Personal/PSK mode.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the TCP three-way handshake used to establish a reliable connection?
questions.note: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client completes with ACK -- establishing a full-duplex TCP session.

explain.correct: The TCP three-way handshake proceeds as: (1) the client sends SYN to initiate; (2) the server replies with SYN-ACK to acknowledge and synchronize; (3) the client sends ACK to confirm, completing the connection setup.
wrong: SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK is incorrect -- ACK alone cannot precede the server's SYN-ACK because no connection exists yet to acknowledge.
SYN-ACK, SYN, ACK reverses the order; the server cannot send SYN-ACK before the client has sent the initial SYN.
ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK is incorrect -- an ACK cannot begin the handshake because there is nothing established to acknowledge yet.

questions.q: What is the correct order of DHCP messages when a client obtains an IP address for the first time?
questions.note: DHCP DORA: the client broadcasts Discover, the server responds Offer, the client broadcasts Request, and the server confirms with Acknowledge.

explain.correct: DHCP follows the DORA sequence: Discover (client broadcasts to find servers), Offer (server proposes an IP), Request (client broadcasts its acceptance), Acknowledge (server confirms the lease). Ports 67 (server) and 68 (client) are used.
wrong: Offer, Discover, Acknowledge, Request reverses the first two steps -- the server cannot make an Offer before receiving a Discover.
Request, Discover, Offer, Acknowledge inverts the sequence; a client cannot send a Request before it has received an Offer.
Discover, Request, Offer, Acknowledge skips the Offer step; the client cannot Request a specific address before the server has proposed one.

questions.q: A DNS query for mail.example.com returns a record pointing to a canonical name. Which DNS record type was returned?
questions.note: CNAME (Canonical Name) maps an alias hostname to the true (canonical) hostname. MX records point to mail server hostnames, not aliases.

explain.correct: A CNAME record creates an alias from one hostname to another (the canonical name). For example, mail.example.com CNAME mailserver.example.com means mail.example.com is an alias for mailserver.example.com.
wrong: An A record maps a hostname directly to an IPv4 address, not to another hostname.
An MX record identifies the mail exchange server for a domain. It specifies a hostname (not an alias relationship), and its priority value determines preference.
A PTR record maps an IP address back to a hostname (reverse DNS lookup), which is the opposite of what was described.

questions.q: A user configures their email client to leave messages on the server so they can access them from multiple devices. Which protocol should they select?
questions.note: IMAP keeps messages on the server and syncs state across all devices; POP3 downloads and deletes from the server by default.

explain.correct: IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) on port 143 (or 993 with SSL) keeps messages stored on the server and synchronizes folder state across all connected devices, making it ideal for multi-device access.
wrong: SMTP is the protocol used to send outgoing email, not retrieve it. Port 25 is the server-to-server relay port.
POP3 on port 110 (or 995 with SSL) downloads messages to the local device and by default deletes them from the server, preventing access from other devices.
FTP is a file transfer protocol unrelated to email retrieval.

questions.q: A network technician runs a command and sees the routing table on a Windows host. Which command produced this output?
questions.note: netstat -r (or route print on Windows) displays the routing table. ipconfig /all shows interface config; arp -a shows the ARP cache.

explain.correct: The netstat -r command (equivalent to route print on Windows) displays the IP routing table, showing network destinations, netmasks, gateways, interfaces, and metrics.
wrong: ipconfig /all displays IP configuration for all network adapters -- addresses, masks, default gateways, DNS servers -- but not the full routing table.
nslookup -type=A performs a DNS query for an A record for a specified hostname; it does not display the routing table.
arp -a displays the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache, showing IP-to-MAC address mappings for recently contacted hosts on the local network.

questions.q: A technician uses single-mode fiber (SMF) to connect two buildings 8 km apart. Why is SMF preferred over multimode fiber (MMF) for this run?
options: SMF uses an LED light source which is safer for long distances
SMF supports longer distances (100+ km) because its smaller core reduces modal dispersion
MMF cannot support distances over 1 km under any standard
SMF uses a larger core that amplifies the signal over distance
questions.note: SMF has a ~9 micron core and uses a laser, enabling 100+ km runs. MMF uses an LED/VCSEL over a 50-62.5 micron core, typically limited to 400-550 m for 10G.

explain.correct: Single-mode fiber has a very small core (~9 micrometers) that allows only one mode of light to propagate, virtually eliminating modal dispersion. Combined with a laser light source, SMF supports distances of 100 km or more, making it the correct choice for an 8 km inter-building run.
wrong: SMF uses a laser light source, not an LED. LEDs are used with multimode fiber because they are cheaper but cannot efficiently couple into SMF's tiny core.

Multimode fiber can support distances beyond 1 km under some standards, but it is limited to roughly 400-550 meters at 10 Gbps speeds due to modal dispersion, which is still insufficient for an 8 km run.
SMF has a smaller core (~9 micrometers) compared to MMF (~50 or 62.5 micrometers). The signal advantage comes from reduced modal dispersion, not core size-based amplification.
